drills.coachNote: Your king marched up to g6, and White's whole army is aimed at it - queen h4, knight g5, and the bishop on c4 staring straight down the c4-f7 diagonal at f7, your king's only real shelter. Rh8 ignores that diagonal completely, so Bxf7# lands at once: bishop takes f7 with check, and with the knight on g5 and queen on h4 covering every escape square, there's nowhere for the king to run. drills.title: vs liwanag22 (867) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: That pawn on g3 is doing more work than it looks: it guards f2, which is exactly what turns ...Qxf2 into mate instead of just check. Your king can't recapture on f2 because g3 covers it, can't step to d3 because his e4 pawn covers that square too, and every other square - d1, d2, e1, e3 - is blocked by your own pieces. Rh1 ignores that pawn entirely, so Qxf2# lands immediately and it's over. Rxg3 was the fix: it removes the one pawn making the mate work and activates your rook; the follow-up (Bd6, Nf1, Qh5+) stays messy, but you're playing on instead of getting mated. When you're already down big, your first job each move is spotting exactly what's threatened.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop on e6 and White's bishop on a2 are staring straight at each other down the same long diagonal, a2 through g8 — that's the feature you missed. Rad8 ignores it, so White plays Bh6 first, forcing g6 to deal with threats near your king, then swoops in with Bxe6 and wins your bishop clean, since the diagonal was never dealt with — fxe6 is just you recapturing the pawn left behind. Since it was your move, Bxa2 simply grabs that bishop first: after Rxa2 Rae8 Ra1 Re6 Bd2 you stay in total control and up huge. When two bishops share a diagonal and it's your move, take first.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c5 has a huge shot sitting right there: Nxc6, forking the black queen on e7 and the rook on d8 at once — the c6 square hits both. Instead a4 lets that moment slip, and Black grabs the initiative with Nxe5, snapping up your knight there, and after Qxe5 Ne4 f3 you're scrambling and the whole 4.5-pawn cushion is gone. Nxc6 wins material outright: after Qd6 Nxd8 Qxd8 Qxg5 Rg8 you've traded a knight for a rook plus a pawn and you're comfortably winning again. When a knight lands on a square attacking two pieces at once, that's the move to find first.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: This is the same shot you missed last move, still sitting on the board: Nxc6, forking the queen on e7 and rook on d8. You played b5 instead, a slower pawn push, and it cost you your knight on e5 — Black's knight on c6 jumps straight into it with Nxe5, and your position unravels from there (bxa6 bxa6 Nb3 is just damage control after the piece is gone), which is your 4.5-pawn swing. Nxc6 removes the exact piece that later captures your e5 knight, and after bxc6 Qd3 Nxc5 bxc5 a5 the trades even out and you keep your edge. Twice in a row here — when a tactic's on the board, cash it in before it disappears.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You have a forced mate on the board and don't see it: Rxf7! clears the way, and after Re2 Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — your rook simply walks up the g-file with the bishop on f6 covering every escape. Instead Qg5 is too slow, and it lets Black's rook on c2 crash into f2, grabbing a pawn and cracking open threats around your own king, which is why Qe5, Rf3, Rf1 shows you suddenly playing defense — that's an 18-pawn swing, from a clean mate to a real fight. When you're this far ahead with the enemy king pinned to the back rank, stop and look for forcing checks before reaching for a quiet move.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Black's queen on b2 is loose in your position and actively eating pawns — that's the danger you need to see, not just your own next idea. Qxc8 was there for the taking, since the rook on c8 simply falls, and after Qb5 Re8 Qf1+ Rxf1 h5 you're simplifying into a position up a full rook. Instead Qd5 ignores the queen on b2 entirely, so Black keeps grabbing — Qxa3, then Qxd4, then Qxh3 — chewing through the pawn shield in front of your own king, and that's how a +19.9 advantage bleeds down 14.9 pawns in a handful of moves. When you're up huge, check what the opponent's most active piece can grab for free before picking your own move.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 is already hanging — Black's pawn on g5 attacks it — and Bf5+ doesn't fix that, it just spends a tempo on a check that's answered easily. Black blocks with e6, gaining time by attacking your bishop again, you retreat with Bc2, and then gxf4 just collects the piece you'd left en prise the whole time — that's your 3.3-pawn swing. The real idea was Nxg5, ripping open the kingside pawns shielding Black's king, which is stuck uncastled on d7 — after fxg5 Bxg5 your bishop lands actively and moves like Qf3 next start hammering straight at that king. With the enemy king stuck in the center like that, look for ways to tear open lines toward it, not a single check that accomplishes nothing.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Before you went hunting for a check, look at your own bishop on f4 — it was hanging the whole time to the pawn on g5. Instead you play the other bishop, Bg6-f5+, but that only costs tempo: Black plays e6, kicks it back to c2, then calmly scoops up your f4 bishop for free with gxf4. You go from equal to down a full piece in three moves. The fix was e4, which ignores the check and hits the center instead — if Black grabs gxf4, you answer exd5, cracking the center open with tempo on his c6 knight. Before hunting for checks, always check what's loose on your own side first.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumps to g5 looking active, but look at the c1-h6 diagonal — White's bishop on c1 stares straight down it, and nothing of yours covers g5. White just plays Bxg5 and the knight is simply gone, no trade, no comeback. From dead equal you're suddenly down a full piece. Nd6 was the move: it retreats to a square that's actually defended, and yes White grabs your e5 pawn with check via Rxe5+, but losing a pawn with check is nothing like losing a piece outright. When a piece has to retreat, ask which square is actually covered, not which square looks most aggressive.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Same problem again — your knight is still sitting undefended on g5, on that same c1-h6 diagonal, and Be7 does nothing about it. White takes Bxg5 a second time and you're bleeding more material on top of what you already gave up. Ne6 was the move both times: get the knight off that diagonal onto a square it can actually stand on. After Ne6, White tries Qf3, you answer Qf6, and even after Nxc6 you get Bxd3 back, keeping things level instead of just handing over pieces. Moving a different piece never makes the piece that's already hanging any safer.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Before pushing e4, notice your bishop on f4 has a better job: Bc7 jumps straight at the queen on d8, forcing Qd7 and seizing the initiative right now. Instead e4 spends a move on the center, and Black answers with Bd7 — a real threat, since that bishop now eyes your b5 pawn along the d7-c6-b5 diagonal. You still get Bc7 in afterward, forcing Qc8, but now b6 isn't a free space-gaining move anymore, it's forced just to save the b5 pawn you let become loose. Same moves, worse order — when you spot a shot like Bc7 hitting the queen, play it before your opponent gets a free tempo to organize against you.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your b5 pawn still has no real support, and Qc3 doesn't fix that — it neither defends b5 nor makes a threat Black has to answer. Black plays Bd7, and once you're forced into Qc5 a move too late, Bxb5 just wins the pawn clean because nothing was ever covering that square. Qc5 right away was the move: it attacks the queen on b6, and after Qd8 you jump the bishop to d6, eyeing the loose knight on e7 along that same diagonal — Re8, Bxe7 wins the piece outright. A queen move that neither defends what's hanging nor threatens something concrete is just a wasted tempo.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Retreating the knight to b7 walks straight into a skewer: White plays Rc7+, your king on c8 has to move, and the rook simply scoops the knight up next with Rxb7 — the piece is gone for nothing. Nf5+ was the shot you needed, because that knight hits both the king on g3 and the rook on g7 at once. White has to deal with the check first with Kf4, and then Nxg7 wins the rook clean, completely flipping the game. Whenever a knight can jump to a square that hits two things at once, especially with check, that's the move to look for before anything quieter.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here, and Rd7 just hangs the rook — it's still on the open d-file with nothing defending it, and White plays Rxd7 and takes it for free. From plus-six you're suddenly in real trouble. Here's the thing: your rook on d8 already had Rxd1 available whenever you wanted it, since White's rook on d1 was just as undefended and wasn't going anywhere. So the move was Bxg3+ first — a free in-between check that nets the g3 pawn since the king must recapture with Kxg3 — and only then Rxd1, cashing in the rook you were already owed. When a piece is yours for free, look for a check that adds extra value before you go collect it.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're up so much material it's tempting to just keep grabbing pawns, but look at the diagonal from your queen on f3 — it runs clean through e4-d5-c6 to b7, and Black's king on e7 has the whole 7th rank wide open behind it. Qxb7+ checks the king along that rank while also forking the rook on a8; Black's only try is Qc7 blocking, and then Qxc7 is mate, king with nowhere to run. Instead exd4 just recaptures a pawn, and after Bg7, dxc5, Qc7, Rd7+ you're still crushing, but you traded a forced mate for a merely-winning position. When you're this far ahead, take the extra few seconds to check for the mating shot before defaulting to the obvious recapture.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Right here you had Rd7+ on the board and reached for the fork instead. Rd7+ is check, and the king's only real escape, e8, is covered by your own knight on f6, so Black is forced into Qxd7 — then Nxd7 scoops the queen for just a rook, a monster trade in a position you were already crushing. Nd7 forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 too, but it's not check, so Black gets a free move: Bg7 tucks the bishop away, and the rook later slides to c8 via Rbc8, and most of that free material slips away. When a check wins material by force, don't settle for a quiet fork that lets your opponent wriggle out.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Before every queen move, trace the lines running through the square you're landing on. Black's queen on e7 sits on the open diagonal e7-f6-g5-h4, and nothing of yours covers h4, so Qxh4 just wins your queen for free. You were already down 4.5 pawns, and handing over the queen turns a bad position into a lost one. Qa3 tucks the queen onto a safe square off that diagonal, and after Re8, c4, d4, g4 you're still generating pawn breaks and real chances instead of playing down a queen. Build the habit of checking every enemy piece's rank, file, and diagonal before you commit to a square.

drills.explanation: Your e5 pawn was attacked by the d6 pawn; exd6 resolves it cleanly, and after cxd6 you develop normally with Nc3 and Nf3, dead level. Pushing e6 instead placed the pawn on a square Black's f7 pawn covers: fxe6 ate it for free, and after Bd3 Nf6 c4 you were simply a pawn down out of the opening.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Watch the f7 pawn — that's exactly what e6 walks into. You already had exd6 available to just resolve the tension on d6, but instead you pushed to e6, where Black's own f7 pawn eats it for free with fxe6, and you get nothing back for it. That's handing over a pawn you didn't need to give up, and it costs you a big chunk of the edge you had. exd6 trades cleanly instead — cxd6 recaptures, and you carry on developing with Nc3, Ne5, Nf3, no material lost. When one of your pawns is hanging or in tension, resolve it by capturing rather than advancing it into another pawn's reach.

drills.explanation: Your queen on e5 was attacked by the knight on f3, and Qe6 was the safe square — it stays active and out of reach, and if Nd4 chases it again, Qe5 returns with White having nothing better than repeating. Qd6 stepped onto the open d-file instead: Rad1 hit the queen with your own rook on d8 lined up behind it, and after Qb4, Rxd8+ Bxd8 handed White the file and the initiative.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: Notice the d-file is wide open, and your queen just walked onto it on d6 with White's rook only one move from lining up on that exact file. Rad1 hits your queen directly since nothing stands between a1 and d6, so you're forced back with Qb4, and then Rxd8+ trades off your rook with Bxd8 the only recapture, leaving your pieces on worse squares for no gain. Qe6 avoids all of it — the queen stays off the open file, and after Nd4, Qe5, Nf3 you're simply repositioning without losing tempo or material. Before putting your queen on a file, check whether an enemy rook is one move from opening onto it.

drills.explanation: Bxb4 just takes a free pawn — the whole point of testing the Polish. White regains it with Bxe5, but after Nf6, c3, Be7 you've swapped his wing pawn for your e-pawn and developed smoothly. Nc6 guarded e5 but walked into b5: the knight had to retreat to e7, and Bxe5 took the pawn anyway — White kept his extra pawn and gained time.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: The pawn on b4 is just sitting there undefended — nothing white touches it — so Bxb4 wins it outright, and it's even check along the b4-e1 diagonal. You played Nc6 instead, which looks like it guards your e5 pawn, but White just plays b5, kicking the knight to e7, and Bxe5 grabs the pawn anyway — your 'defense' lasted one move. So the pawn you were protecting falls regardless, and the free pawn on b4 got away for nothing. Bxb4 takes the material immediately, and after Bxe5, Nf6, c3, Be7, d4 you're doing fine, having traded pawns evenly instead of losing one for free. Grab a hanging piece the moment you see it.

drills.explanation: Nd4 does everything at once: it saves the knight from the d5 pawn and attacks White's queen on f3, winning a free tempo. After Qd1 you follow with Bf5 and b5, developing with real energy. Nce7 retreated to a passive square that blocks your own f8 bishop, and gave White time for d4, building a big centre unchallenged.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c6 is attacked by the pawn on d5, but d4 lets it escape the attack while also hitting White's queen on f3 — that's the move, Nd4, forcing Qd1 and buying you the tempo to play Bf5. Instead you played Nce7, a passive retreat that only solves the safety problem, and White just builds with d4, your queen ends up awkwardly placed on d6, and after Ne2 you're only just now getting Nf6 in while White's grabbed the bigger center. When a piece is attacked, look first for a square that both escapes and creates a threat of its own, not just the nearest safe retreat.
